questions.topic: Reading a first-difference column
questions.learningObjective: compute the first differences of a short list of values
questions.practice: forming first differences from a table of values
questions.stem: A list of consecutive values is 3, 11, 19, 27, 35, 43. What is the common value of the first differences of this list?
questions.explanation: The first differences of a list are found by subtracting each entry from the one after it. Doing that here gives 11 minus 3, which is 8, then 19 minus 11, which is 8 again, then 27 minus 19, again 8, then 35 minus 27, again 8, and finally 43 minus 35, again 8. Five consecutive subtractions all give the same result, so the first differences are constant at 8, and the list is arithmetic with common difference 8. This is the simplest fact a difference table records, and it is the reason a list with constant first differences can be modelled by a straight-line formula. The check matters: a single equal pair of differences proves nothing, which is why five differences that all agree is worth far more than one coincidence.
questions.hint: Subtract each entry from the next one and look at the five results rather than at the list itself.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Constant first differences mean a linear rule
questions.learningObjective: connect constant first differences to a polynomial of degree one
questions.practice: identifying the degree suggested by a difference pattern
questions.stem: A list of values has all of its first differences equal to the same constant. What can be concluded about the rule that produced it?

options.text: the values come from a quadratic rule, because any rule that grows steadily must be quadratic
options.misconception: conflates steady growth with a quadratic, ignoring that a linear rule also grows steadily

options.text: the values come from a geometric rule, since each value is 8 more than the one before it
options.misconception: mistakes a constant additive increase for a constant multiplicative one, which is the geometric test

options.text: the values come from a linear rule, because a polynomial of degree 1 has constant first differences
the values come from an exponential rule, because a constant difference cannot persist for long
options.misconception: claims the additive pattern must eventually fail, with no basis in the algebra of a linear rule

questions.explanation: The difference table of a polynomial settles the question by itself. A polynomial of degree 1, written a times n plus b, has first difference exactly a at every step, because subtracting a(n+1) plus b from an plus b removes the b and leaves a. Since the first differences are all equal, the leading term cannot be of degree 2 or higher: any term of degree 2 or more would survive the subtraction and force the differences to change. So the rule is linear in n. The same reasoning extends, and this is the useful general form: if the k-th differences are constant then the rule is a polynomial of degree k, because differencing lowers the degree of a polynomial by exactly one. A caution is needed about reading this backwards, since constant first differences certify a linear rule, but a list whose first differences merely look similar may still come from something else entirely.
questions.hint: Subtracting a times n plus b from a times n plus a plus b removes the constant, so a linear rule has constant differences.

The first differences of 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49 are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, which increase by 2 each time, and the second differences are therefore all 2. Because the second differences are constant, the rule is quadratic, and the last first difference can be extended by the same 2, giving 15 as the next first difference. Adding 15 to the last value, 49, gives 64. Nothing here assumes the values are squares, though they are, and the method would work just as well on a list such as 2, 3, 6, 11, 18 whose rule is n squared minus n plus 2. What makes the step safe is the constant second difference, since without it there would be no rule for extending the first differences.

questions.topic: Degree from where the differences settle
questions.learningObjective: read the degree of a polynomial rule off the difference table

questions.stem: When a difference table is built from a list of values produced by a polynomial rule, how is the degree of that rule identified?

options.text: the rule has degree 3, because the third differences are the first ones to become constant
the rule has degree 1, because the values themselves still increase steadily
options.misconception: judges the degree by whether the values grow, which every rule of any degree does

options.text: the rule has degree 2, because the second differences are already constant for a cubic
options.misconception: confuses the second differences of a cubic, which are linear and not constant, with a constant row

options.text: the rule has degree 4, since four rows of differences were needed before anything settled
options.misconception: counts the rows computed rather than the row that is constant, which is what identifies the degree

questions.explanation: Differencing a polynomial of degree d produces a polynomial of degree d minus 1, because the leading term of the difference is d times a times n to the power d minus 1, so one power drops at every step. Applying that repeatedly, the d-th differences of a degree d polynomial are the constant d times a times d factorial, and the rows below that are zero. The degree is therefore the index of the first row that is constant, and that is the row you read off the table. For the rule 2n cubed minus n the first differences are 1, 13, 43, 91, 157, 241, the second are 12, 30, 48, 66, 84, the third are 18, 18, 18, 18, and it is the third row that is constant, so the degree is 3, matching the cubic term. Counting rows without finding the constant one is the usual error, since the number of rows is one more than the degree.
questions.hint: Each differencing step drops the degree by one, so the degree is the position of the first constant row.

questions.topic: Second differences recover the leading coefficient
questions.learningObjective: recover the coefficient of n squared from a constant second difference
questions.practice: reading the leading coefficient off a difference table
questions.stem: The values 4, 14, 32, 58, 92 and 134 are the first six values of a quadratic rule of the form a n squared plus b n plus c. What is the value of a?
questions.explanation: The first differences of 4, 14, 32, 58, 92, 134 are 10, 18, 26, 34, 42, and the second differences are 8, 8, 8, 8. For a rule a n squared plus b n plus c the first difference is a of 2n plus 1 plus b, so the second difference is the constant 2a and nothing of b or c survives. Here that constant is 8, so 2a equal to 8 gives a equal to 4. The rest of the rule can then be pinned down from two values: at n equal to 1 the rule gives 4 plus b plus c, which must be 4, so b plus c is 0, and at n equal to 2 it gives 16 plus 2b plus c, which must be 14, so 2b plus c is minus 2. Subtracting leaves b equal to minus 2 and then c equal to 2, giving the rule 4n squared minus 2n plus 2, and that reproduces 32, 58, 92 and 134 exactly. So the leading coefficient really is 4, and the difference table is a reliable way to get it without ever writing the rule down first.
questions.hint: The constant second difference of a n squared plus b n plus c is 2a, so divide the 8 by 2.

questions.stem: A list built from a quadratic rule reads 1, 4, 9, unknown, 25, 36, 49 in that order. One entry has been lost. What is the missing value?
questions.explanation: The known values fix the second difference: 1, 4 and 9 give first differences 3 and 5, so a second difference of 2, and 25, 36 and 49 give 11 and 13, again a second difference of 2. The rule therefore has constant second difference 2, which is the signature of a quadratic, and the missing entry must bridge the gap consistently. Work forward from 9 with second difference 2: the first difference out of 9 is 5, and the next one is 5 plus 2, which is 7, so the missing value is 9 plus 7, that is 16. Work backward instead from 25: the first difference into 25 is 13, the one before it is 13 minus 2, which is 11, and the missing value is 25 minus 11, which is also 16. Two independent directions agreeing on 16 is the check that the recovery is sound, and a single value such as 17 or 15 would break one of the two second differences.
questions.hint: The second difference is 2, so the first differences near the gap are 5 and 7, and the missing value is 9 plus 7.

questions.topic: Third differences recover the leading coefficient
questions.learningObjective: recover the coefficient of n cubed from a constant third difference
questions.practice: reading a cubic's leading coefficient off its third differences
questions.stem: The third differences of a list produced by a rule of the form a n cubed plus lower terms are all equal to 12. What does that imply about a?

options.text: a is 2, because the third difference of a n cubed is 6a and 6a equal to 12 gives a equal to 2
a is 12, because the constant third difference is the leading coefficient itself
options.misconception: forgets the factor of 3 factorial that the three differencing steps contribute

options.text: a is 72, because the leading coefficient is the constant multiplied by 3 factorial rather than divided by it
options.misconception: inverts the factorial factor, multiplying by 6 where the rule divides by it

options.text: a is 3, because the third difference of a n cubed is 4a rather than 6a
options.misconception: confuses the factor for a quartic, which is 4 factorial and so 24a, with the cubic factor

questions.explanation: Work the degree down one step at a time. Differencing a n cubed gives a leading term 3a n squared, so the second differences carry 3a n, and the third differences carry 6a, a constant. Everything of lower degree has been annihilated along the way, since the first difference of a constant is 0, so the constant third difference reports the leading coefficient and nothing else. Setting 6a equal to 12 gives a equal to 2. The factor is a factorial, and the sequence of factors is worth keeping: the first difference of a n is a, the second of a n squared is 2a, the third of a n cubed is 6a and the fourth of a n to the fourth is 24a. A quick numerical check confirms it, since the rule 2n cubed plus anything lower has third differences that are 2 times 6, that is 12, whatever the lower terms are.
questions.hint: The third difference of a cubic with leading coefficient a is 6a, so solve 6a equal to 12.

questions.topic: Recovering a missing value from third differences
questions.learningObjective: recover a missing entry of a cubic list from its constant third differences
questions.practice: solving a difference equation for a missing term
questions.stem: A list built from a cubic rule reads 1, 8, 27, unknown, 125, 216, 343 in that order. What is the missing value?
questions.explanation: Write the unknown entry as m and build the difference rows symbolically. The first differences are 7, 19, m minus 27, 125 minus m, 91 and 127. The second differences are then 12, m minus 46, 152 minus 2m, m minus 34 and 36. The third differences, which must be constant for a cubic, are m minus 58, 198 minus 3m, 3m minus 186 and 70 minus m. Setting the first two of these equal gives m minus 58 equal to 198 minus 3m, so 4m is 256 and m is 64. The remaining two third differences confirm it, each becoming 6, which is the constant third difference of a cubic with leading coefficient 1. As a shortcut with the arithmetic done, the values on either side of the gap, 27 at position 3 and 125 at position 5, are two steps apart, and two steps of a cubic with second differences growing by 6 each step is exactly the pattern that puts 64 between them.
questions.hint: Build the rows symbolically with the unknown entry m, then set the first two third differences equal to solve for m.

options.text: a is 24, because the constant row of a difference table is exactly the leading coefficient

The numbers 1, 2, 6 and 24 appearing in successive rows are factorials, and that is the whole content of the pattern.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Why the spacing has to be regular
questions.learningObjective: explain why a simple difference table requires equally spaced inputs
questions.practice: identifying the hypothesis behind a difference table
questions.stem: A difference table is built from values a rule takes at a list of inputs. What condition on those inputs does the method require, and why?

options.text: the values have to be positive, since differences of negative values are not defined
options.misconception: believes differences are undefined for negative entries, when subtraction works for any reals

options.text: the number of values has to be a multiple of four, so that every difference row has the same length
options.misconception: invents a length requirement that has no basis; rows shorten by one at every step by design

options.text: the values have to be integers, since a fractional difference cannot be trusted
options.misconception: restricts to integers for no algebraic reason, as decimal differences work exactly as well

options.text: the steps of n have to be equally spaced, because each difference subtracts the value one step earlier and the pattern of gaps is what the arithmetic needs

questions.explanation: Every entry of a difference row is formed by subtracting the value at one input from the value at the next input, and the next row repeats that on the results. If the gaps between inputs are all the same size h, then the arithmetic that reduces a polynomial by one degree each time works unchanged, and the constant rows appear as expected. If the gaps differ, the same formal subtraction still produces numbers, but they no longer correspond to a clean derivative-like operation, the constant rows do not appear, and the leading-coefficient rule picks up factors of h. For instance with gaps of 2 the second difference of a n squared becomes 8a rather than 2a, since each differencing step contributes its own factor of the step size. Unequal gaps are not hopeless, they are simply handled by the divided-difference method, where each entry divides by the actual distance between the two inputs.
questions.hint: Each difference compares inputs one step apart, so a constant step is what makes the degree-drop rule work unchanged.

The first differences of 1, 8, 21, 40, 65 are 7, 13, 19 and 25, and the second differences are all 6, so the first differences form an arithmetic progression with common difference 6. The rule settles the matter independently: 3 times 0 squared minus 2 times 0 is 0. questions.topic: Newton's forward difference formula
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a quadratic rule between two of its table values
questions.practice: applying the forward difference formula at a fractional step
questions.stem: A quadratic rule takes the values 3, 9, 19, 33 and 51 at the inputs 1 through 5. Using the forward difference formula, find its value at input 2.5, which falls between two of the listed inputs.
questions.explanation: The forward difference formula gives the value at input u, where u counts steps from the first input, as the first value plus u times the first difference plus the falling product u of u minus 1 over 2 times the second difference, with no higher terms because the second differences are constant. Here the first value is 3, the first difference is 6 and the second difference is 4. The wanted input 2.5 is 1.5 steps past input 1, so u is 3 over 2, and the falling product u of u minus 1 is 3 over 2 times 1 over 2, which is 3 over 4, so dividing by 2 gives 3 over 8. The value is 3 plus 3 over 2 times 6, that is 3 plus 9, plus 3 over 8 times 4, that is 3 over 2, giving 13.5. The rule confirms it independently, since 2 times 2.5 squared plus 1 is 12.5 plus 1, which is 13.5. This is the situation the formula was designed for, an input that is not on the table at all.
questions.hint: u is 1.5 steps from the first input, so use 3 plus 1.5 times 6 plus the product 1.5 times 0.5 over 2 times 4.

options.text: the last entry plus v times the last first difference plus v of v plus 1 over 2 times the last second difference, where v is the wanted input minus the last input and so is negative for an input before the table
the first entry plus v times the first difference plus the binomial coefficient v over 2 times the first second difference, with v counting forward from the first input

The value is the last entry plus v times the last first difference plus the product v of v plus 1 over 2 times the last second difference. A quadratic needs only the value row and the first two difference rows, and both ends of the table contain them, which is why the choice of end is a matter of convenience. questions.explanation: Work from the far end. The last value is 129, the last first difference is 129 minus 99, which is 30, and the last second difference is 4. Define v as the wanted input minus the last input, so v is 3.5 minus 8, which is minus 4.5. The formula is 129 plus v times 30 plus the product v of v plus 1 over 2 times 4. The first correction is minus 4.5 times 30, that is minus 135. The second uses the product minus 4.5 times minus 3.5, which is 15.75, divided by 2 to give 7.875, times 4 to give 31.5. The total is 129 minus 135 plus 31.5, which is 25.5. The rule confirms it, since 2 times 3.5 squared plus 1 is 24.5 plus 1, which is 25.5. The negative value of v is not a trick but the mechanism, since it is what makes the two corrections partially cancel and land the answer outside the range of the table rather than beyond it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Why the top row of a table is constant
questions.learningObjective: explain why the third differences of a cubic rule form a constant row and what it equals
questions.practice: justifying the constant row of a difference table algebraically
questions.stem: Explain why the third differences of any rule of the form a n cubed plus b n squared plus c n plus d are constant, and state what that constant is in terms of a.

answer.exemplar: The whole argument rests on one binomial expansion, worked through once. The forward difference of a monomial is the polynomial (n plus 1) to the power m minus n to the power m, and the binomial theorem says the leading surviving term is m times n to the power m minus 1, because the n to the power m terms cancel and the next coefficient is the binomial coefficient m over 2 multiplying n to the power m minus 2. So taking a forward difference drops the degree by exactly one and multiplies the leading coefficient by the degree that was dropped. Now apply the rule three times to the cubic a n cubed. The first difference leads with 3a n squared, the second with 3a times 2 times n, that is 6a n, and the third with 6a times 1, that is 6a, a constant. The lower terms do not interfere, because the first difference of a constant is 0, so the contributions from b n squared, c n and d have all been annihilated by the time the third difference is taken, and what survives is the leading term alone. The same chain gives the general result that the d-th difference of a times n to the power d is a times the factorial of d, that is a, 2a, 6a and 24a for degrees 1, 2, 3 and 4. Two consequences organise the reading of a table. First, a constant row at position d certifies a degree d rule, because a rule of higher degree would leave a non-zero row further down, and a rule of lower degree would have had a zero row at position d instead. Second, the value of the constant row pins the leading coefficient, since dividing it by the factorial of d recovers a. Together these turn a list of numbers into a statement about the rule that produced them.

questions.explanation: The binomial expansion is the whole argument, and applying it three times turns a cubic into a constant while killing every lower-degree term on the way, so the constant that survives is a multiple of the leading coefficient alone.
questions.hint: Expand (n plus 1) to the power m minus n to the power m: the leading n to the power m terms cancel and m times n to the power m minus 1 survives, so each step drops the degree by one and multiplies the coefficient by the degree.

questions.explanation: Summing and differencing undo each other, so a claim of the form the sum equals some expression is equivalent to a claim about differences. questions.explanation: The building blocks that suit an operation are the ones the operation respects. Each differencing step therefore lowers k by one and multiplies by k, which is precisely the behaviour that makes the constant row of a table appear at the degree of the rule. Any polynomial of degree at most d is a linear combination of the d plus 1 falling products of lengths 0 to d, so the choice loses no generality, and it is the basis in which a difference table is already written. The plain powers n, n squared and so on also span the same space, but differencing them mixes the terms, so the coefficients of a table are not the coefficients of the rule.

The identity to check is n squared equals 2 times n times n minus 1 over 2 plus n, which is n times n minus 1 plus n, and expanding the right side gives n squared minus n plus n, which is n squared. Testing at a single input confirms the constants: at n equal to 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is 2 times 0 plus 1, which is 1; at n equal to 4 the left side is 16 and the right side is 2 times 6 plus 4, that is 16. The reason to make this rewrite at all is that the coefficients in it are exactly the leading entries of the difference table, so a table becomes a statement about the rule rather than about a particular stretch of its values.
questions.hint: n squared is n times n minus 1 plus n, and n times n minus 1 is 2 times the binomial coefficient n over 2.

questions.topic: Differences of the binomial coefficients
questions.learningObjective: state the difference rule for the binomial coefficients
questions.practice: applying the falling-product rule to a binomial coefficient
questions.stem: The binomial coefficient n over 3 lists 0, 0, 1, 4, 10, 20, 35 and so on as n runs from 1 upwards. What is its first difference?

options.text: the binomial coefficient n over 3, since differencing a binomial coefficient leaves it unchanged
options.misconception: believes the operation is the identity, which no difference operation ever is on a growing list

options.text: n cubed over 6 divided by n over 1, since the leading term falls by one power of n
options.misconception: divides two binomial coefficients instead of using the falling-product rule, which relates them by a single product

options.text: 1, since the third difference of a cubic is constant and the second difference of a quadratic is too
options.misconception: confuses the two binomial coefficients with the constant rows of difference tables

options.text: the binomial coefficient n over 2, since the first difference of the n over 3 is the n over 2

questions.explanation: The binomial coefficient n over 3 is the falling product of three factors divided by 3 factorial, and the difference rule for falling products says that the first difference of the k-factor product is k times the (k minus 1)-factor product. Applying that with k equal to 3 gives three times the falling product of two factors over 3 factorial, which is three times n times n minus 1 over 6, that is the binomial coefficient n over 2. The lists make the same point: the first differences of 0, 0, 1, 4, 10, 20, 35 are 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, and the binomial coefficient n over 2 runs 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, the same numbers one place along. Two further differences reduce to the binomial coefficient n over 1 and then to 1, so the whole column of binomial coefficients is one table, which is why sums of binomial coefficients and the identities built on them can all be read off a difference table rather than proved from scratch.
questions.hint: The n over 3 is a three-factor falling product over 3 factorial, and its first difference is three times the two-factor product over 3 factorial, which is the n over 2.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: How many rules fit three points
questions.learningObjective: state the uniqueness of interpolation once the degree is fixed
questions.practice: counting the rules that pass through three equispaced points
questions.stem: Three values of a rule are known, at inputs 0, 1 and 2, with values 1, 3 and 6. Assuming the rule is a polynomial of degree at most 2, how many such polynomials pass through all three points?

options.text: exactly one, the quadratic through the three points, and a higher degree would fit them as well unless the degree is fixed in advance
infinitely many, since any polynomial of degree 3 or more can be bent to pass through three points
options.misconception: ignores the hypothesis that the degree is fixed, which is what makes the polynomial unique

options.text: exactly three, one for each pair of points, which are then all checked against the third
options.misconception: counts candidate curves rather than surviving ones, and none of the pairwise fits passes through the third point

options.text: none, unless the three points happen to lie on a rule whose second differences are equal
options.misconception: believes the second differences must already be equal, when that is a property of the answer rather than a requirement on the data

questions.explanation: Once the degree is capped there is exactly one polynomial, and the reason is that a degree d polynomial has d plus 1 coefficients, so a quadratic has three unknowns and three conditions pin them down. Here the conditions are 1 at 0, 3 at 1 and 6 at 2, and the difference table does the job directly: the first differences of 1, 3, 6 are 2 and 3, the second difference is 1, so the leading coefficient is 1 over 2, and the rule is n squared over 2 plus 3n over 2 plus 1. What the table also shows is why the degree cap matters, since the numbers 1, 3, 6 are the triangular numbers and a cubic could be fitted to three points with a free parameter, and so could any higher degree. The same data therefore supports an infinite family of polynomial rules unless the degree is stated, and this is the single most important qualification in interpolation: uniqueness is a statement about a space of candidate rules, not about the data alone.
questions.hint: A quadratic has three coefficients and the three data give three equations, so the system is determined; without the degree cap there would be infinitely many.

questions.topic: Interpolating between two table values
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a quadratic rule halfway between two of its table values
questions.practice: using the forward difference formula at a half step
questions.stem: A quadratic rule takes the values 5, 9, 15, 23 and 33 at the inputs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. What is its value at input 2.5?
questions.explanation: This is interpolation, and the forward difference formula is the tool. The first value is 5, the first difference is 4 and the second difference is 2, and the wanted input is 1.5 steps past the first input, so u is 3 over 2. The value is 5 plus u times 4, that is 5 plus 6, plus the product u of u minus 1 over 2 times 2, and the product 3 over 2 times 1 over 2 is 3 over 4, so dividing by 2 gives 3 over 8, times 2 gives 3 over 4. The total is 11 plus 3 over 4, which is 11.75. The rule behind the list is n squared plus n plus 3, and at 2.5 that is 6.25 plus 2.5 plus 3, which is 11.75 as well, so the two routes agree. A remark on what interpolation does and does not claim is worth making here: the value at 2.5 is forced by the three nearest data points together with the assumption of degree at most 2, and that assumption is the only reason there is a single answer.
questions.hint: Use 5 plus 1.5 times 4 plus the product 1.5 times 0.5 over 2 times 2, which is 11.75.

questions.topic: Why equal spacing matters for interpolation
questions.learningObjective: state the hypothesis on which the simple difference table depends
questions.practice: deciding whether a data set can use the plain difference method
questions.stem: The forward difference formula and the simple difference table both rely on an assumption about the inputs at which the values were recorded. What is it?

options.text: the gaps have to be whole numbers, because the binomial coefficients in the formula are only defined for whole steps
options.misconception: confuses a restriction on the step with a restriction on the step size, and fractional steps are perfectly well defined

options.text: the gaps have to be decreasing, so that the later rows compare ever closer inputs
options.misconception: invents a direction for the gaps, when only their equality matters

options.text: the gaps have to be equal, because each difference then compares inputs a fixed step apart and the degree drops by one at every row
the gaps do not matter at all, since a table can be built from any set of inputs
options.misconception: overstates the method, since a table of plain differences from unevenly spaced inputs does not behave as claimed

questions.explanation: Both methods compare values at inputs a fixed step apart, and everything they claim follows from that step being the same each time. The degree of a polynomial drops by one per difference row only because the step is uniform, and the constant row appears at the position given by the degree only for the same reason. With a step of 2 the second difference of a n squared is 8a rather than 2a, since each of the two differencing steps contributes a factor of the step size. Unevenly spaced inputs are not hopeless, they simply need a different object, the divided difference, in which each entry divides by the actual distance between the two inputs involved. The divided difference of a polynomial of degree d is still constant at level d, and the Newton interpolation formula built on divided differences is the standard tool for arbitrary input sets. So the equal-spacing assumption is a convenience that buys a much simpler table, not a limitation of what interpolation can do.
questions.hint: Each difference compares inputs a fixed step apart, so a uniform step is what makes the degree drop by exactly one per row.

questions.topic: Selecting the polynomial that fits three points
questions.learningObjective: identify which of several candidate polynomials passes through three given points

questions.stem: Four candidate polynomials are proposed for a rule whose values are 1 at input 0, 3 at input 1 and 6 at input 2. Which of them pass through all three points? Select all that apply.

options.text: one half of x squared plus 3 halves of x plus 1, which gives 1, 3 and 6 at the three inputs
x squared plus x plus 1, which is a simpler expression but gives 1, 3 and 7
options.misconception: prefers the simpler-looking expression and never substitutes the three inputs to check it

options.text: one half of x squared plus one half of x plus 1, which has the right leading coefficient but the wrong linear one
options.misconception: fixes the leading coefficient from the second difference and then guesses the rest instead of solving for it

options.text: 2x squared plus x, which has no constant term and so cannot give the value 1 at input 0
options.misconception: assumes a rule through three points must have no constant term, having not substituted at input 0

questions.explanation: Substituting each input into each candidate settles the question, and only one survives. For one half of x squared plus 3 halves of x plus 1: at 0 the value is 1, at 1 it is one half plus 3 halves plus 1, which is 3, and at 2 it is 2 plus 3 plus 1, which is 6, so all three points are matched. For x squared plus x plus 1 the values are 1, 3 and 7, so the third point fails even though the first two match, which is the trap: two points are not enough. For one half of x squared plus one half of x plus 1 the values are 1, 2 and 4, so it fails at the second and third inputs. For 2x squared plus x the values are 0, 3 and 10, failing at the first and third. Since a degree d polynomial is determined by d plus 1 points, only one polynomial of degree at most 2 can pass through three points, so the survival of exactly one candidate is the expected outcome rather than a coincidence.
questions.hint: Substitute all three inputs into each candidate; the values at 0, 1 and 2 must be 1, 3 and 6.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Evaluating a Lagrange interpolation formula
questions.learningObjective: compute a value from the Lagrange form of an interpolating polynomial
questions.practice: evaluating a Lagrange interpolation formula by hand
questions.stem: Use the Lagrange interpolation formula for the three points with input 0 and value 1, input 1 and value 3, and input 2 and value 6. What is the value of the interpolating polynomial at input 4?
questions.explanation: The Lagrange form writes the polynomial as a sum with one term per data point, and the term for a point is its value multiplied by the product of the ratios of the wanted input to the other inputs over that point's own distances to them. For the point at 0 with value 1 the term is 1 times (4 minus 1)(4 minus 2) over (0 minus 1)(0 minus 2), that is 3 times 2 over 2, which is 3. For the point at 1 with value 3 the term is 3 times (4 minus 0)(4 minus 2) over (1 minus 0)(1 minus 2), that is 3 times 4 times 2 over minus 1, which is minus 24. For the point at 2 with value 6 the term is 6 times (4 minus 0)(4 minus 1) over (2 minus 0)(2 minus 1), that is 6 times 4 times 3 over 2, which is 36. The total is 3 minus 24 plus 36, which is 15. The structure is worth noticing, since at the data points the terms collapse to 0 and 1 in turn, so each of the three points is reproduced exactly, and at any other input all three terms are genuinely present.
questions.hint: Each term is the value at a node times the ratio of products over that node's own distances; the three terms are 3, minus 24 and 36.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The denominator in a Lagrange term
questions.learningObjective: state which distances form the denominator of a Lagrange term
questions.practice: diagnosing a malformed Lagrange formula
questions.stem: A student writes the interpolating term for a point at input a as the value at a multiplied by the product over all nodes of the wanted input minus the node, divided by the product of a minus every node including a itself. What is wrong?

options.text: the denominator should use the wanted input instead of the node, since the ratios are measured from the evaluation point
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the node and the evaluation point, which is the other plausible form of the formula

options.text: the denominator of each term must use only the other two nodes, not all three, so the term for the point at 0 is over (0 minus 1)(0 minus 2) and not over (0 minus 1)(0 minus 2)(0 minus 0)
the numerator should use the node's own coordinate instead of the evaluation point
options.misconception: inverts the ratio in the numerator, which gives a polynomial that does not pass through the data

options.text: no denominator is needed at all, since the ratios cancel when the three terms are added
options.misconception: believes the normalisation is redundant, when each term must be exactly 1 at its own node and 0 at the others

questions.explanation: The denominator of a Lagrange term is built from the distances from its own node to the other nodes, and the node's distance to itself is 0, so including it divides by 0. The reason the other nodes are used is the normalisation: at the node's own input the numerator is also 0, that is the product of a minus each of the other nodes, which cancels the denominator and leaves the value itself, and at any other node's input one factor of the numerator vanishes while the denominator does not, leaving 0. So each term gives its own data value at its own data point and 0 at the other two, and the sum of the terms reproduces every data value exactly. This is the property that makes the form a genuine interpolant rather than merely an expression of the right degree, and dropping a factor from the denominator destroys it. A quick check on any candidate term is to substitute the three inputs and confirm that the row of results holds one recorded value and two zeros.
questions.hint: Substitute the three inputs: a term must give the recorded value at its own node and 0 at the other two, which forces the denominator to use only the other nodes.

questions.topic: Divided differences at unevenly spaced inputs
questions.learningObjective: compute the Newton form from divided differences at unevenly spaced inputs

questions.stem: A rule is recorded at the uneven inputs 0, 2 and 5 with the values 1, 5 and 16. First compute the first and second divided differences, then use them to find the value of the quadratic through the three points at input 3.

options.text: the first divided differences are 2 and 11 over 3, the second is 1 over 3, and the value at input 3 is 1 plus 2 times 3 plus 1 over 3 times 3 times 2, which is 9
options.misconception: uses the wrong product in the Newton term, taking the steps as 3 and 2 rather than 3 and 1 from the first node

options.text: the first divided differences are 4 and 11, the second is 7 over 5, and the value at input 3 is 6
options.misconception: divides the value changes by 1 rather than by the input changes, which is the mistake uneven spacing is meant to prevent

options.text: the first divided differences are 2 and 11 over 3, the second is 1 over 3, and the value at input 3 is 1 plus 2 times 3 plus 1 over 3 times 3 times 1, which is 8
the second divided difference is 1 over 5, since it is the change in the first divided difference over the distance 5 minus 0
options.misconception: divides by 5 alone and forgets to subtract the two first divided differences first, dropping the whole second level

questions.explanation: A divided difference divides by the actual distance between the two inputs involved, which is what lets the method cope with uneven spacing. The first divided difference between the first two points is the change in value over the change in input, that is 5 minus 1 over 2 minus 0, which is 2. Between the second and third points it is 16 minus 5 over 5 minus 2, that is 11 over 3. The second divided difference is the change between these two quantities over the distance between the outer inputs, that is 11 over 3 minus 2 over 5 minus 0, which is 5 over 3 divided by 5, that is 1 over 3. The Newton form then reads the value at any input as the first value plus the first divided difference times the step from the first input plus the second divided difference times the product of the two steps. At input 3 the steps from the first node are 3 and 1, so the value is 1 plus 2 times 3 plus 1 over 3 times 3 times 1, which is 1 plus 6 plus 1, and the total is 8. The leading coefficient of the resulting rule is that second divided difference, 1 over 3, which matches the one third that the equispaced difference table produced for the same data.
questions.hint: First divided differences are 2 and 11 over 3; the second is 1 over 3, so the value at 3 is 1 plus 2 times 3 plus 1 over 3 times 3 times 1.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Risks of extrapolating a table
questions.learningObjective: explain why a polynomial fit beyond the data is not trustworthy
questions.practice: judging whether an extrapolation can be relied on
questions.stem: Explain why extending a difference table beyond the last recorded value is a weaker kind of prediction than interpolating between recorded values, and describe a setting in which the difference goes from harmless to serious.

answer.exemplar: The two operations use the same arithmetic and carry very different amounts of information, and the difference is about which values are actually being reproduced. An interpolation lies between recorded points, so the polynomial in question is already forced to match data that were really observed, and every entry of the difference table it rests on is anchored to a measurement. An extrapolation asks the polynomial to continue past the region where any evidence exists, so the only thing constraining it is the pattern detected in the table. That pattern carries a real assumption, namely that the rule really is polynomial of the degree the table reported, and nothing in the data can confirm the assumption outside the recorded range. The failure is usually gradual and then sudden. A quadratic fitted to three values of a quantity that is really exponential will agree closely at first, because near any point a smooth function looks almost like a low-degree polynomial, and then the two diverge more and more, since the fitted polynomial flattens or turns over while the exponential keeps bending upwards. A concrete illustration is the following: the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 have first differences 1, 2, 4, 8 and second differences 1, 2, 4, so the second differences are not constant, which already warns that no polynomial rule is in hand. If a student nevertheless fits a quadratic to the first three values, the differences 1 and 2 give a second difference of 1 and so a leading coefficient of one half, which yields the rule n squared minus n plus 2 all over 2, and at input 10 that rule predicts 46 while the real list gives 512. No arithmetic error was made anywhere in that prediction, and the gap between the two numbers is the whole of the danger. Three habits make the distinction usable in practice. First, count the data and ask whether the degree is forced; a degree d fit needs d plus 1 points, and a table built from fewer cannot support the degree the pattern suggests. Second, prefer an interpolation to an extrapolation whenever the choice exists, and say plainly in any report which of the two has been done. Third, treat a table that refuses to settle as information rather than as an obstacle, since the refusal is itself the warning that the extrapolation has no rule behind it.

questions.explanation: Both operations use the same arithmetic, so the difference between them is entirely about evidence: an interpolation sits between recorded values that already pin the rule down, while an extrapolation continues past every recorded value and rests only on the assumption that the pattern holds there.
questions.hint: An interpolation is anchored to observed values, while an extrapolation is anchored only to a detected pattern, and the degree the pattern suggests may not survive outside the data.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Interpolation against extrapolation
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a prediction inside the data range from one beyond it
questions.practice: choosing between interpolating and extrapolating
questions.stem: A set of recorded values is used to predict a value of the same quantity. What distinguishes interpolation from extrapolation?

options.text: an interpolation is a prediction inside the range of recorded inputs, where the data already constrain the rule, while an extrapolation goes beyond every recorded input
an interpolation is more accurate because the arithmetic is easier, while an extrapolation needs more work
options.misconception: confuses computational convenience with evidential support, which is the whole distinction here

options.text: an interpolation uses the forward difference formula and an extrapolation uses the backward one
options.misconception: describes a choice of technique as though it were a choice of evidential strength

options.text: there is no difference between them, since a polynomial that fits the data continues them by the same algebra
options.misconception: claims continuity of the algebra implies equal reliability, ignoring where the evidence stops

questions.explanation: The distinction is about where the wanted input sits relative to the recorded ones, not about which formula is used. An interpolation asks for a value inside the range of the data, so the polynomial in question is pinned by observations on both sides of the wanted point, and the prediction is a matter of reading off a curve that the data already constrain from every direction. An extrapolation asks for a value beyond every recorded input, so on one side of the point there is no evidence at all, and the prediction rests entirely on the assumption that the pattern continues. The practical consequence is that an interpolation error stays small when the data are accurate, while an extrapolation error can be large even when it is small, because the rule may change character just past the last measurement. Two refinements are worth knowing: an interpolation between two nearby points is safer than one between distant ones, and an extrapolation one step out is safer than one many steps out, since nothing about the rule is checked at any point in either case.
questions.hint: Ask where the wanted input lies relative to the recorded inputs: between them, or beyond all of them.
